lesson.title: Wandering Genes: How Migration Reshapes Populations
lesson.summary: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations through migrating individuals or dispersing gametes, and it is the fifth and final way real populations violate the Hardy-Weinberg assumption of a closed, isolated gene pool.
lesson.body:
Gene flow is the transfer of alleles from one population to another, carried by individuals who move and then breed in a new location, or by gametes that disperse on their own, such as pollen carried by wind or insects between plant populations. It directly violates the last of the five Hardy-Weinberg assumptions: no migration into or out of the population. In population genetics terms, gene flow connects gene pools that would otherwise drift apart on their own, which means understanding it requires thinking not just about allele frequencies within a single population, but about how those frequencies compare between two or more populations that may differ from one another.

The general effect of gene flow is to make populations more genetically similar to each other. If a population on one side of a mountain range has a high frequency of a particular allele, and a few individuals cross the range each generation and successfully breed with the population on the other side, that allele's frequency on both sides tends to converge over time. This makes gene flow something of a counterforce to both genetic drift and local natural selection. Drift and selection can each push a population's allele frequencies away from those of its neighbors, in different directions and for different reasons, while ongoing gene flow keeps pulling separated populations back toward genetic uniformity. Populations connected by substantial gene flow tend to evolve together. Populations cut off from gene flow are free to diverge.

A wolf that disperses from one pack's territory and breeds into a neighboring, geographically separate wolf population is a straightforward example of gene flow through migration. Wind pollinated plants show the same principle without any individual actually relocating: pollen grains, each carrying half a plant's genome, can travel considerable distances and fertilize flowers in a population far from the parent plant. In both cases, the key requirement is not just movement but successful reproduction afterward. An individual that migrates but never breeds in its new location has not contributed to gene flow at all. This last point matters later in this unit. When gene flow between two populations is reduced or cut off entirely, whatever other forces are acting on each population, drift, selection, mutation, are free to push them apart without gene flow pulling them back together, which is often the first step toward two populations becoming genetically and reproductively distinct.
